**The Weight of Silence**

The room was too quiet. Not the kind of quiet that comes after a storm, when the air still hums with the memory of thunder, but the kind that settles like dust over forgotten things. It pressed against my ears, thick and suffocating, as if the walls themselves were holding their breath.

I sat on the edge of the bed, my fingers tracing the edge of a photograph that had long since lost its corners to time. The faces in it were blurred, their features softened by the years, but I knew them. I knew the way my mother’s laugh sounded like wind chimes in a summer breeze, the way my father’s hands were always warm, even in winter. I knew the way they had looked at me the last time I saw them—before the car, before the hospital, before the funeral home, before the empty house that now echoed with the ghosts of their absence.

I should have been used to the silence by now. Three years. Three years since the phone call that shattered everything. Three years of waking up to an alarm that no longer needed to be set, of eating meals that tasted like ash, of staring at a ceiling that never once asked how I was doing. But silence, I’ve learned, is a shape-shifter. It wears many faces. Sometimes it’s the quiet of a Sunday morning, the kind where the world holds its breath just to see if you’ll break. Other times, it’s the kind that comes in the middle of the night, when the dark is so complete you can hear your own heartbeat, and you wonder if it’s possible to die from the weight of it.

I closed my eyes and tried to remember the sound of their voices. My mother’s voice, soft and melodic, like a lullaby I could never quite recall. My father’s voice, deep and steady, the kind that made you feel safe even when the world was falling apart. But the memories were slipping, fraying at the edges like an old sweater. All I could hear now was the silence, pressing in from all sides, a living thing that had taken up residence in my chest.

I thought about calling someone. A friend. A therapist. My sister, who lived three states away and only called on birthdays and holidays because that was the rule now. But my fingers stayed still on the phone screen, frozen. What was there to say? *I’m lonely.* *I miss them.* *I don’t know how to do this anymore.* Those words felt too heavy, too raw. Like if I spoke them aloud, the silence would swallow me whole.

Instead, I stood and walked to the window. Outside, the world was moving—cars hummed down the street, people hurried past with their coffee and their problems, their lives still unfolding in ways mine never would again. I envied them, briefly. Not for their happiness, but for their ability to keep going. To fill the silence with something other than grief.

I thought about writing. A letter. A story. Anything to make the silence bearable. But the page stayed blank, taunting me. What was there to say that hadn’t already been said a thousand times before? That love doesn’t end when people do? That some wounds never close, they just scab over and itch forever?

I sat back down on the bed, the photograph still clutched in my hand. Maybe that was the problem. Maybe I was holding on too tightly to the past, to the people who were gone, to the life that no longer existed. Maybe the silence wasn’t the enemy. Maybe it was just the space where I needed to learn how to breathe again.

I set the photograph down on the nightstand, where it belonged. Not in my hands, not in my heart, but somewhere safe. Somewhere I could look at it when I was ready, and not feel like I was drowning.

Then I turned on the radio.

The music was too loud at first, jarring against the quiet I had grown so used to. But slowly, it filled the room. It filled my chest. It filled the hollow places where grief had carved out its home.

I closed my eyes and let it wash over me.

Maybe silence wasn’t the enemy after all. Maybe it was just the space between the notes. The pause that made the music matter. The quiet that reminded me I was still here. Still alive. Still fighting my way back to the surface.

And for now, that was enough.
